item.title: Software developers are the target. New trojan attacks supply chains and inflicts multifaceted damage on infected PCs
item.description:
A multi-stage trojan targeting C++ and C# developers weaponizes Visual Studio project files, infected executables, and Python scripts to poison supply chains and deploy a backdoor, stealer, clipper, and cryptominer on the same host.
- Three-phase loader chain: Trojan.DownLoader49.35384 uses PEB walking and initterm hijacking to run a hidden PowerShell command. Phase 2 (Trojan.DownLoader49.35687) checks for sandbox via mutex Global\PFNMX, then pulls C2 addresses from Steam profiles and a GitHub raw file at raw.githubusercontent[.]com/XxXloverXxX/rustflare/refs/heads/main/crates/engine (Base64 plus XOR), then injects into one of 41 System32 processes and passes the C2 over named pipe pipe\VccFrameworkchannel.
- Phase 3 BackDoor.Siggen2.5906 persists by replacing Discord's profapi.dll, Edge's domain_actions.dll and well_known_domains.dll, and dropping C:\Windows\omadmapi.dll with the phase 2 payload (bungee.boo). UAC bypass via ms-settings COM hijack using a random .vbs in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\.
- Stealer targets Discord tokens, browser credentials and cookies, Telegram Desktop folders, and Exodus wallets. The Exodus app.asar is replaced with a trojanized index.js (Trojan.Siggen32.44702) downloaded from balista[.]lol, intercepting wallet recovery phrases. A clipboard monitor also swaps crypto wallet addresses in real time.

item.title: Anatomy of a helpdesk social engineering attack (and how to stop MFA bypass)
item.description:
Scattered Spider and copycat actors are bypassing MFA entirely through helpdesk social engineering, not malware. AI-assisted voice cloning and PII scraping have made this attack chain nearly frictionless in 2026.
Key findings:
- Attack chain: recon via data brokers and LinkedIn builds a PII profile, then a caller impersonates the employee, defeats knowledge-based verification, and convinces helpdesk to reset the password and re-enroll MFA to an attacker-controlled device. No exploit, no malware, just a phone call.
- Once inside the cloud account, threat actors scrape emails for credentials, pivot to document shares, send fraudulent invoices to suppliers, or use residential proxies to blend sessions so the access looks entirely routine, including satisfied MFA on an enrolled device.
- If only a password reset is obtained, push bombing follows: flooding the real user with approval prompts until one is accepted, or calling helpdesk back to have the login manually approved.
- Detection still exists even after a clean social engineering call: MFA device enrollment events, impossible travel, new device sign-ins, and off-hours resets all surface in cloud telemetry. Correlate those signals rather than waiting for a single alert.
Treat MFA re-enrollment as a privileged action requiring manager approval or callback to a pre-enrolled number, never PII alone. Migrate toward FIDO2 or passkeys to eliminate push bombing and SIM-swap risk entirely.

item.title: GigaWiper Merges Three Malware Families Into One Destructive Backdoor
item.description:
GigaWiper merges three malware families into a single Go backdoor combining espionage, remote control, and on-demand disk destruction. Microsoft discovered it during active wiping activity in October 2025.
- Built in Go, GigaWiper communicates via RabbitMQ on port 5544 for command delivery and Redis on port 7542 for results, both pointing to C2 at 185.182.193[.]21. A RabbitMQ fanout exchange named "All" can blast destruction commands to every infected host simultaneously, while a "Topic" exchange enables targeted tasking.
- Persistence lives in a scheduled task named "OneDrive Update" firing every minute and at startup, with execution count tracked in a registry key disguised as a OneDrive entry. Command 19 wipes Windows event logs using two separate deletion methods if the first fails, directly targeting forensic visibility.
- The destructive command set covers raw disk overwrite (Command 1), BSOD plus boot file deletion (Command 2), fake ransomware with .candy extension and irrecoverable encryption (Command 3, derived from Crucio ransomware), and a multi-pass zero/0xFF/random wipe of the Windows drive (Command 12, a Go port of FlockWiper). No ransom note exists because recovery was never intended.

item.title: This new Windows malware can take over your PC and wipe it clean
item.description:
GigaWiper, a modular Golang backdoor for Windows, blends espionage, remote access, and multi-method data destruction in a single framework observed in intrusions since October 2025.
Key findings:
- Built from prior tools: GigaWiper wraps Crucio ransomware and FlockWiper disk wiper into one platform, implementing roughly 20 commands across three categories: destruction, remote access/monitoring, and system management. The fake ransomware module encrypts files then discards the key, making recovery impossible.
- Destruction methods include raw disk overwrite with forced reboot, multi-pass Windows drive wipe using alternating byte patterns, and the Crucio-based encryption-without-key wiper. Once any of these execute, recovery is effectively off the table.
- Persistence via a scheduled task named "OneDrive Update" running every minute and at startup (T1053.005). Remote control runs over a TCP desktop-streaming server that self-carves Windows Firewall exceptions to stay reachable.
- C2 infrastructure: 185.182.193[.]21 and 212.8.248[.]104. Malwarebytes detects components as Trojan.FlockWiper and Backdoor.GigaWiper.
Responder priority: GigaWiper lands post-compromise, so timeline your initial access before it matters. Hunt for the "OneDrive Update" scheduled task, review firewall exception logs for attacker-added rules, and check for connections to those C2 IPs. On detection, isolate immediately and assume destructive commands may have already been queued.

item.title: The AI Agent Credential Crisis: From Stealer Log to Source Code
item.description:
Stealer logs now target AI coding agents, turning a single infected developer machine into a key for source code, cloud infra, and CI/CD pipelines. Over 3.1 million OpenAI credentials were compromised in 2025 alone.
Key findings:
- SOCRadar analyzed stealer log data across 2025 and found 3.1M+ records tied to OpenAI, with total AI/developer platform exposure exceeding 3M accounts. Replit (204K) and Hugging Face (186K) followed, platforms where credentials carry write access to repos, datasets, and deployment pipelines. Three malware families, LummaC2 (56%), RedLine (17%), and StealC (13%), account for 86% of all observed logs.
- The multiplier effect is the core risk. A stolen AI agent credential is not one account. It bundles OAuth tokens for GitHub/GitLab orgs, AWS/GCP/Azure keys, CI/CD pipeline tokens, package registry creds, and MCP integrations for Slack, Jira, and Sentry into a single harvested session. Infostealers harvest .env files, .claude/settings.json, and browser-synced session cookies without distinguishing personal from corporate devices.
- The quarterly curve tells a disruption story. Q1 peaked at 953K records, then a May 2025 law enforcement action against LummaC2 C2 infrastructure drove a 42% volume drop through Q3 (553K). By Q4, volumes recovered to 857K as operators rebuilt and newer families like Acreed and MacSync filled the gap. Temporary wins, not structural defeat.

item.title: 222 GitHub Repositories Linked to Fake Go Package Malware Operation
item.description:
222 GitHub repositories across 190 accounts delivered loaders, Vidar infostealer, AsyncRAT, and XMRig miners via fake Go packages, tracked by Socket as Operation Muck and Load.
- The pivot artifact is a GitHub Actions workflow email: ischhfd83@rambler[.]ru. Every repo used the same email with force-push automation running on a per-minute schedule to manufacture fake commit history, even as visible usernames rotated per account. That email is a cluster fingerprint linking this to earlier Sophos-documented backdoor campaigns.
- The initial Go module (github[.]com/kaleidora/dnsub-scanning-tool) ran a hidden PowerShell command before any scanner logic, downloading from muckcoding[.]com, decoding via certutil, and executing L.ps1 with -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. L.ps1 uses Base64 plus XOR layers and dead-drops payload URLs via Pastebin, Telegram, YouTube, Google Docs, and GitCode using a marker string "LastW". Encrypted blob SHA-256: 51cada347262d7b2bcde70552fcdae221625ad75435cee8a9c3e7b67cc47a807.
- Payloads land in C:\ProgramData\Windows.Microsoft.Photos as Microsoft.exe, signed by Exodus Movement Inc., not Microsoft. A 7-Zip binary stages at C:\ProgramData\zipathh\7zrr.exe. Post-execution behavior includes Defender and UAC tampering, scheduled task persistence, browser data access, and WriteProcessMemory/SetThreadContext calls consistent with process injection.

item.title: Dell BIOS Passwords: Weak XOR Encryption Allows Recovery from SPI Flash (CVE-2026-40639)
item.description:
CVE-2026-40639: Dell BIOS passwords stored under reversible XOR encryption in SPI flash, recoverable in milliseconds with a chip programmer. Actively unpatched on the Wyse 5070 thin client as of today.
Key findings:
- Dell's SystemPwSmm SMM driver stores BIOS admin/user passwords as XOR-encrypted data in the DVAR region of SPI flash, not a hash. The first byte is stored in cleartext. For passwords up to 12 characters, null-padding in the 32-byte field leaks the entire 20-byte key directly. No brute force needed.
- The key is derived from mostly device-static data plus the cleartext first byte, meaning only 256 possible keys exist per device. DVAR is log-structured, so deleted password records persist on flash. A short historical password with the same first character hands you the key to decrypt a longer current one.
- Confirmed vulnerable: Latitude E7250, Latitude 7490, XPS 15 9560, Wyse 5070. Not vulnerable: OptiPlex 3000 and newer models using SIVB with SHA-256. DSA-2026-197 patches Edge Gateway and Precision lines; the Wyse 5070 and confirmed-vulnerable Latitudes are not in that first wave. Dell targets remaining fixes by end of July 2026.
- CVSS 3.1 scored 5.7 by Dell (AV:P/AC:H), 6.1 by researchers (AV:P/AC:L). Physical access to flash is required via SOIC clip or attacker-controlled OS boot. Impact: disables Secure Boot, changes boot order, and can break TPM-backed BitLocker chains if unmeasured settings are modified.

item.title: How WP-SHELLSTORM Exposed 1.4M WordPress Sites
item.description:
A Chinese-linked webshell access brokerage left its entire operation exposed for 22 days, revealing 1.4M+ targeted domains, 27 weaponized CVEs, 5,700+ active webshells, and a parallel enterprise Java credential-theft campaign.
- On June 11, 2026, SOCRadar found an unauthenticated Python SimpleHTTPServer at 137.175.93[.]126 exposing ~800MB across 434 files: webshells, exploit scripts, scan results, bash history, and C2 config. Attribution points to a Chinese-speaking financially motivated group (WABO), based on Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 code comments, FOFA usage (requires Chinese 🇨🇳 phone registration), and handles "tance"/"chen-kk" in the exposed filesystem.
- Five weeks before the WordPress blitz, the same actor ran a two-day Nacos campaign exploiting CVE-2021-29441 (send "Nacos-Server" User-Agent header, skip auth entirely), exfiltrating 613 config files from 11 victims across fintech, logistics, and gaming. Stolen data included AWS/Alibaba/Oracle Cloud credentials, production DB strings, Alipay RSA private keys, and JWT secrets.
- The primary webshell down.php (SHA256: 84F7E396A48913851A10CC78C5CC22A25634564ABD0694465236D2F365E2BDEE) runs four obfuscation layers before unpacking a full BestShell-derived implant. VShell persistence renames its process to [kworker/0:2] to blend into Linux kernel thread listings. At 13:30:44 UTC June 11, 24 IPs pulled the same payload in one second, confirming active botnet C2.

item.title: Conditional Access Misconfigurations Exposed 55 Orgs with MFA On
item.description:
Two separate M365 campaigns bypassed MFA across 64+ orgs by exploiting Conditional Access blind spots: device code phishing via Railway PaaS and ROPC credential spray via LSHIY LLC's IPv6 range.
Key findings:
- Railway campaign (March 2026): EvilTokens PhaaS weaponized OAuth device code flow (T1528), harvesting tokens from legitimate Microsoft endpoints. Railway's clean IP reputation defeated Identity Protection risk scoring. Three Railway IPs drove ~84% of attack traffic across 344 orgs in the US 🇺🇸, Canada 🇨🇦, Australia 🇦🇺, New Zealand 🇳🇿, and Germany 🇩🇪. Tokens persist up to 90 days, surviving password resets.
- LSHIY campaign: 81 million ROPC requests hit the /token endpoint directly, bypassing the authorization endpoint entirely. MFA Conditional Access never fired because Azure CLI was excluded. 55 of 78 compromised accounts had active MFA policies, yet were still breached.
- CA policy failures observed: MFA scoped to specific apps not "All Cloud Apps," group-scoped policies missing compromised accounts, trusted location mislabeled as US-based, and one tenant with a policy explicitly named "Block Azure CLI" that did not block Azure CLI.
- Detection opportunity: hunt Azure AD sign-in logs for successful authentications where clientAppUsed equals "Device Code" or "ROPC" and cross-reference against accounts not in legacy auth exception groups.
Audit your CA policies against All Cloud Apps, All Users, All Client App Types.

item.title: Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)
item.description:
AI coding agents across six major platforms can be tricked into writing attacker SSH keys or shell configs via symlink-poisoned repos, no memory corruption required. The GhostApproval research from Wiz exposes a decades-old primitive wearing a new disguise.
Key details:
- The attack chain stacks three failures: prompt injection via README instructions aimed at the agent, symlink traversal without path resolution, and a confirmation dialog that shows the friendly filename (project_settings.json) while hiding the real target (~/.ssh/authorized_keys or ~/.zshrc). Remove any one link and the attack fizzles. Git stores symlinks with file mode 120000, blob content is the raw target path, and recreates them faithfully on clone on Linux and macOS.
- Six agents tested: Amazon Q Developer, Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf. All showed variations of the flaw. In several, the write completed before a confirmation dialog appeared. In the Claude Code case, the agent's own internal reasoning correctly identified the real target file, then the dialog told the human it was editing "project_settings.json." CWE-61 covers the symlink following; CWE-451 covers the UI misrepresentation. AWS, Google, and Cursor shipped fixes.
- Prior art matters for scoping: CVE-2024-32002 abused symlinks plus submodules to drop into .git/hooks and execute code on git clone --recurse-submodules.

item.title: Not-so-anonymous telemetry: The @injectivelabs/sdk-ts backdoor
item.description:
Supply chain attack hit @injectivelabs/sdk-ts v1.20.21, stealing BIP-39 seed phrases and raw private keys from a finance-focused blockchain SDK with ~175,000 monthly downloads. Window of exposure: 49 minutes.
- Malicious commit 0121928 was pushed July 8 at 8:24 p.m. UTC directly to the main branch, appearing to originate from a legitimate maintainer's account. Git metadata showed the commits came from a UTC-4 timezone machine never previously used by that committer, a forensic signal suggesting account compromise or session hijacking rather than a rogue insider.
- The attack hooked PrivateKey.fromMnemonic() and PrivateKey.fromHex() inside packages/sdk-ts/src/core/accounts/PrivateKey.ts. Every time a wallet loaded, the full 12/24-word seed phrase or raw private key string was passed to trackKeyDerivation(), base64-encoded, and smuggled in the X-Request-Id HTTP header to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective[.]network, a domain crafted to blend with legitimate Injective gRPC infrastructure. The exfil endpoint was still live at time of writing.
- Deception was layered: the new file carried a convincing docblock describing anonymous SDK telemetry and timing metrics, and the C2 domain was built at runtime from a character-code array to resist static analysis.
- Only @injectivelabs/sdk-ts version 1.20.21 is confirmed malicious. Versions before 1.20.21 and 1.20.23 onward are clean.

item.title: CitrixBleed 2 (CVE-2025-5777) 7Steps to Dragonforce Ransomware | Huntress
item.description:
CVE-2025-5777 "CitrixBleed 2" is being actively exploited by an IAB to steal live NetScaler sessions, escalate to SYSTEM via a registry symlink primitive, and deploy DragonForce ransomware, all in under an hour across multiple unrelated orgs.
- CVE-2025-5777 is a pre-auth memory overread in NetScaler ADC/Gateway. A burst of malformed POST requests to /p/u/doAuthentication.do with an empty login field leaks ~127 bytes of heap per request, including live session tokens. MFA is irrelevant once a token is stolen and replayed. Forensic proof lives in ns.log: 5,000+ AAA LOGIN_FAILED events with binary garbage in the User field is leaked heap, not a spray. A session active from an attacker IP with zero successful logins is the smoking gun.
- Printer mappings are a gift. Citrix auto-creates client printer entries in the Windows Application log, embedding the attacker's workstation name. WIN-4E0AP4JTJR9 and WIN-VI960VQI4I6 appeared case after case. Pivot between Microsoft-Windows-TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager/Operational (source IP plus session ID) and MetaFrameEvents (session ID to client name) to fingerprint the operator's machine.
- Privilege escalation uses a REG_LINK registry symlink planted under the RdpBus device class GUID, redirected into GPO-List\test. gpupdate forces a SYSTEM-context write through the link; sc start AppMgmt detonates it.

item.title: The Two BIOS Passwords Everyone Confuses
item.description:
"We set the BIOS password" is not a complete sentence. Setup password and boot password protect different things, and mixing them up leaves firmware-level gaps on every machine in the fleet.
Key findings:
- The setup (administrator) password gates firmware config changes: Secure Boot state, boot order, TPM, IOMMU. It does NOT prompt at power-on. A stolen laptop with only this set boots straight to the OS. The boot (power-on) password is what stops the machine from starting at all. One password does not cover the other.
- Vendor naming makes this worse. Lenovo calls them Supervisor + Power-On, Dell calls them Admin + System, HP calls them BIOS Administrator + Power-On. A policy or ticket that says "set the BIOS password" has not actually specified which control was configured.
- Setting the admin password does not automatically lock configuration changes. There is a separate setting to prevent boot-order and Secure Boot edits when an admin password is present. Miss it and the password is half the control it should be.
- Eclypsium's flash-dump research found at least one vendor storing the admin password in plaintext ASCII in a firmware variable, and another using a short, truncated hash built from a static key, making it crackable offline and identical across every unit of that model.
Audit state, not policy. Read the actual password-set flag per device via /sys/class/firmware-attributes/ on Linux or vendor WMI namespaces on Windows.

item.title: Finding SOCKS with Proxywatch
item.description:
SpecterOps releases Proxywatch, a behavior-based open-source tool to detect SOCKS proxy pivots, C2 beaconing, and tunneling activity on live endpoints without relying on static signatures or process-port baselines.
- SOCKS proxy pivoting lets attackers run tools like Impacket, nmap, or netexec entirely from their own machine through a compromised host, meaning no new processes spawn on the victim, no attacker tooling touches disk, and EDR parent-child detection models see nothing. C2 frameworks like Cobalt Strike, Sliver, and Mythic all support this natively. This is why registry persistence created via Impacket reg.py over SOCKS gets missed: the code never executes on-target.
- Proxywatch runs on Linux and Windows, reading /proc/net/tcp and /proc/<pid>/fd on Linux, and GetExtendedTcpTable plus CreateToolhelp32Snapshot on Windows. It builds per-process behavioral profiles using 83 signals including loopback usage, multiplex relay patterns, callback cadence, jitter measurement, writable-path binaries, and named pipe C2 patterns, then assigns roles: control-channel, control-pivot, listener, or outbound.
- In a live demo, cheerful_glove.exe (a Sliver beacon) was flagged control-pivot via signals pivot-multiplex-relay and pivot-non-loopback-internal. A separate beacon, beacon-j.exe, was caught via a 75-second callback pattern with 0.44 jitter, unsigned binary, and suspicious-exe-path (C:\Users\ops\Desktop\testing\).

item.title: GigaWiper: Anatomy of a destructive backdoor assembled from multiple malware
item.description:
GigaWiper is a Golang backdoor that merges three separate destructive malware families into a single modular implant, observed wiping targets since October 2025.
- GigaWiper combines a raw disk wiper, a Crucio ransomware-derived fake encryptor (command 3, .candy extension, keys never saved), and a reimplemented FlockWiper secure multi-pass wiper (command 12) as discrete C2 commands. C2 runs over RabbitMQ (AMQP) and Redis with AES-encrypted config; observed C2 IPs are 185.182.193[.]21 and 212.8.248[.]104.
- Persistence lands via a scheduled task named "OneDrive Update" (runs every minute plus at startup) and tracks execution count in HKCU\SOFTWARE\OneDrive\Environment. Command 19 clears System, Setup, Application, and Security event logs, including a direct delete of C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx if wevtutil fails.
- Code overlap links GigaWiper to Crucio (CISA advisory, Dec 2023) via shared BigBangExtortMain function, and to FlockWiper (VirusTotal, June 2025) via PDB paths referencing "GRAT" and identical execution flow, suggesting one actor built all three tools.
- IOC hashes (4 backdoor, 1 standalone wiper, 1 Crucio, 2 FlockWiper) and both C2 IPs are in the Microsoft report. Microsoft Defender detections include WprFlock, WprCree, FlockWiper, and GigaWiper signatures.
Hunt for the "OneDrive Update" scheduled task, outbound AMQP/Redis to the listed IPs, and Golang PE files in unexpected paths.

item.title: Hiding in the Chain: Multi-Stage LNK Attack Leveraging TON Blockchain to Deliver Node.JS Backdoor
item.description:
Multi-stage LNK attack uses TON blockchain as a C2 resolver and drops a Node.js backdoor, making traditional domain-based blocking ineffective against this campaign.
Key findings:
- Initial access via a malicious ZIP containing a .lnk file. When executed, the shortcut fires a hidden PowerShell command (T1059.001) that downloads a legitimate node.exe binary and deploys a Node.js backdoor, blending malicious traffic with a trusted runtime.
- The malware uses EtherHiding (T1102): querying the TON blockchain to retrieve the live C2 address. Blocking a domain or IP does nothing here because the C2 pointer lives on an immutable ledger, not a registrar-controlled hostname.
- DFIR artifact focus: hunt for node.exe spawned from unusual parent processes (PowerShell, explorer, or a user temp path), LNK files in ZIP archives in user download or temp directories, and outbound connections to TON API endpoints from non-developer endpoints.

item.title: Januscape: 16-Year-Old Linux KVM Bug Enables Cloud VM Escape Attacks
item.description:
CVE-2026-53359 "Januscape": a 16-year-old use-after-free in Linux KVM's shadow MMU lets a guest VM crash or potentially escape to the host, affecting both Intel and AMD x86 clouds exposing nested virtualization.
- CVE-2026-53359 lives in kvm_mmu_get_child_sp(), where KVM matched shadow page candidates by memory address alone, ignoring the page role type. A guest with root can race the shadow MMU until host kernel memory is corrupted. The public PoC reliably panics the host, taking every co-tenant VM down with it. A full code-execution exploit exists but has not been released.
- Attack prerequisites: root inside the guest (standard on any rented cloud VM) plus nested virtualization exposed by the host. item.title: The HTTP 303 SSRF Hack : From Python HTTP Client Defaults to AWS Credential Exfiltration.
item.description:
A blind SSRF escalated to live AWS IAM credential theft by chaining a user-controlled OAuth field, Python requests default redirect handling, and IMDSv1 reachability on an EKS node. No single component was broken. The composition was.
- BigQuery service account JSON accepted by the platform contained a user-supplied token_uri field with zero allowlist validation. The backend passed it verbatim to the google-auth library, which POSTed a signed JWT to whatever URL the attacker provided. An OOB Interactsh probe confirmed the primitive immediately.
- Direct SSRF to 169.254.169[.]254 failed because IMDS returns HTTP 405 to POST requests. Timing analysis (IMDS responded in 0.34s vs. 28s for an unroutable IP) proved the pod could reach IMDS, the verb was simply wrong. The fix: serve HTTP 303 See Other from an attacker-controlled server. Per RFC 7231 §6.4.4, Python requests rewrites POST to GET on a 303, strips the body, and follows the Location header to IMDS.
- The error reflection channel completed the read primitive. google-auth parsed the IMDS JSON response, failed to find access_token, raised an exception, and the worker returned the raw exception string, including AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and SessionToken, in the HTTP 400 body to the authenticated caller.
- Remediation: the platform implemented a frozenset allowlist at the field-parsing layer, blocking any token_uri not matching oauth2.googleapis[.]com/token or accounts.google[.]com/o/oauth2/token.

Key findings:
- CVE-2025-14179 (High) hits pdo_firebird's php_firebird_preprocess tokenizer. The quoting routine PDO::quote works correctly, but when the rebuilt SQL string passes through php_firebird_alloc_prepare_stmt, a strncat() call truncates on the first NUL byte (\0), dropping the closing quote of a string literal. Attacker input escapes the quoted context and is parsed as executable SQL. The exploit pattern: quote with PDO::quote, pass to PDO::prepare, inject \0 in the first parameter, then place a UNION SELECT payload in the second. Fixed in commit 3f40b65 by replacing strncat() with a binary-safe length-bounded copy.
- CVE-2025-14180 (Moderate, CVSS 6.3) affects pdo_pgsql when PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES is true. A parameter containing an invalid multibyte sequence (e.g. alice\x99) causes libpq's PQescapeStringConn to set the error flag and the driver returns NULL. The PDO parser then evaluates ZSTR_LEN(NULL), dereferencing address 0x0, delivering SIGSEGV and killing the PHP worker instantly. The try/catch block never fires because the crash is at C level.

item.title: RCE via Gemini Live AI Voice Session Misconfiguration.
item.description:
Gemini Live API ephemeral tokens default to fully unconstrained sessions, letting any authenticated browser client inject tool definitions including Python code execution via a malicious setup frame.
Key findings:
- The BidiGenerateContentConstrained WebSocket endpoint only enforces what the backend encodes in live_connect_constraints at token mint time. If that field is absent, the server accepts the client's setup frame verbatim, including arbitrary model, system_instruction, and tools values. The official google-gemini/gemini-live-api-examples reference ships without live_connect_constraints, so every team following it ships this misconfiguration.
- The exploit chain is three steps: register a free account, intercept the POST to the session creation endpoint and confirm bidi_generate_content_setup is absent from the response, then connect to the WebSocket and send a setup frame enabling codeExecution. Server replies setupComplete and the session runs under attacker-defined parameters.
- Code execution lands in a gVisor sandbox (kernel 4.19.0-gvisor, UID 369346771). Outbound TCP, DNS, and persistent writes are blocked. No path to internal systems without a gVisor escape. Real impact: unbounded compute consumption billed to the API account owner.
- Detection opportunity: proxy or log the token mint response from your own backend. Absence of bidi_generate_content_setup in that response is the single indicator. No WebSocket inspection needed.

item.title: Exploiting Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD)
item.description:
RBCD exploitation gives any user with write access to a computer object a clear path to full machine takeover via Kerberos delegation abuse, no Domain Admin required.
Key details:
- The attack abuses msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on the target computer object. Any principal with write rights over that attribute, including the object's creator, can configure RBCD. Default MachineAccountQuota lets any authenticated user add up to 10 computer accounts, supplying a ready-made SPN-bearing "Service A" with no special privileges needed.
- The chain: create a rogue computer account (addcomputer.py or Powermad), write RBCD trust to the target with rbcd.py, call S4U2Self to get a non-forwardable ticket for Administrator, then S4U2Proxy to exchange it for a cifs ticket, and pass it with psexec.py, secretsdump.py, or smbclient.py.
- RBCD's critical difference from classic constrained delegation: the KDC accepts a non-forwardable evidence ticket as long as the target resource's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity trusts the requestor, bypassing the FORWARDABLE check that blocks classic delegation abuse.
- Artifact focus: query AD for unexpected values in msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity on workstations and servers, and audit newly created computer accounts (Event ID 4741). Rubeus and getST.py leave Kerberos S4U activity in KDC logs (Event ID 4769) with unusual delegation fields.

item.title: The Blind Spot in the Watchtower: Detections for When Someone Attacks Your Sentinel
item.description:
Microsoft Sentinel has no built-in watch over itself: nine KQL detections close the blind spot attackers exploit to disable rules, cut log feeds, and erase their own incidents before any alert fires.
Most SOC teams have hundreds of detections aimed outward at endpoints, email, and identity. Almost none watch the SIEM itself. A capable attacker does not start loud. They reach for the recorder first.
- Sentinel stores its own audit trail across three tables: AzureActivity (free, all resource changes), _SentinelAudit() (rule-level before/after diff, requires health and audit feature enabled), and _SentinelHealth() (confirms rules are actually running). All nine detections pull from one of these three sources.
- The attack surface is wider than most teams realize: disabling or deleting an analytic rule (_SentinelAudit, hourly schedule), shortening table retention or dropping a table (AzureActivity WORKSPACES/TABLES/WRITE or DELETE), killing a data connector or DCR (DATACONNECTORS or DATACOLLECTIONRULES operations), deleting diagnostic settings (DIAGNOSTICSETTINGS/DELETE, a known evasion Microsoft templates for), granting a Sentinel Contributor or Owner role outside the approved list (ROLEASSIGNMENTS/WRITE), tampering with playbooks, watchlists, or automation rules, editing or closing incidents by unauthorized callers, and deleting the workspace or its resource lock outright.
